bodyHtml:
API 653 scope in detail: where the standard starts and stops

API 653 covers carbon and low-alloy steel atmospheric tanks after they have been placed in service, from the foundation up to the face of the first flange on each nozzle. New-tank design and construction belong to API 650; API 653 takes over once the tank is operating and governs where the two appear to conflict.

Put in our own words, the scope works like this. API 653 applies to carbon and low-alloy steel tanks originally built to API 650 or to the older API 12C. It sets the minimum rules for keeping those tanks sound once they are operating, whether their seams are welded or riveted, provided they are non-refrigerated and run at essentially atmospheric pressure. Physically, it reaches from the foundation through the bottom, shell, structure and roof to attached appurtenances, and along each nozzle as far as the first flange face, first threaded joint or first welding-end connection. Piping beyond that point is normally handled under the owner's piping programme, usually API 570 (source: API standards catalogue; confirm wording in your licensed copy).

Two scope rules matter day to day. API 650 design, welding, examination and material rules are applied when an in-service tank is repaired or altered, but where the two documents appear to conflict, API 653 governs for tanks in service. And because API 653 follows the principles of API 650, an owner/operator may choose to apply it to any steel tank built to a recognised tank specification, which is how many operators handle older or non-API tanks.

API 653 does not cover refrigerated tanks or pressurised spheres and bullets, which fall under pressure-vessel rules. Small shop-built tanks are often managed under a different industry standard such as STI SP001. Where the original construction standard gives no detail and API 653 is silent, users are directed to details that give integrity equal to the current edition of API 650.

Edition note: the current publication is the fifth edition with its addenda and errata. Addendum 4 (July 2025) revised the text on tank-bottom plate thickness, and API lists a further revision in development. Free copies found online are usually much older editions, so do not take intervals, tables or clause numbers from them. Check API's catalogue and your licensed copy before quoting an edition in a procedure or contract.

Who does what: owner, inspection agency, inspector, engineer, examiner

The owner/operator carries ultimate responsibility for compliance. An authorized inspector, employed by an authorized inspection agency and certified under the standard's inspector annex, directs the formal inspections and evaluates the tank. NDE examiners, storage tank engineers and repair organisations each have defined roles beneath that.

The roles are worth spelling out, because confusion here causes most procurement and audit problems:

  • Owner/operator. The legal entity that controls the tank and its operation. It has ultimate responsibility for complying with API 653, sets the inspection programme, keeps the records and decides on repairs, re-rating or retirement.
  • Authorized inspection agency. The organisation (an owner/operator's own inspection group, an insurer, or an independent agency, depending on jurisdiction and definitions in the standard) that employs the authorized inspector.
  • Authorized inspector. An employee of an authorized inspection agency who is certified as an aboveground storage tank inspector under the standard's certification annex. In the United States that certification is the API 653 credential issued by API ICP. External and internal inspections are formal inspections directed or supervised by the authorized inspector, and for internal inspections the inspector responsible for evaluating the tank must conduct a visual inspection and assure the quality and completeness of the NDE results.
  • Storage tank engineer. One or more people knowledgeable and experienced in the engineering disciplines associated with tank design, fabrication and evaluation. Engineering judgments such as approving a hydrotest exemption or certain repair details sit here.
  • NDE examiners. The technicians who perform ultrasonic thickness readings, floor scanning, magnetic particle, penetrant, radiography and vacuum-box testing. API 653 requires NDE personnel and acceptance criteria to follow API 650 plus any supplemental requirements in API 653; in US practice that usually means technicians certified under an employer written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A.

A contractor can take every reading on a tank and still not be the inspector of record. When you buy "an API 653 inspection", make sure the scope names the authorized inspector and says who is only performing NDE.

Internal inspection intervals: what changed between editions

The internal interval is the most edition-sensitive part of API 653. The logic has stayed the same: the bottom must not fall below the minimum thickness at the next inspection. The tables, credits and caps have changed, and Addendum 4 (July 2025) revised the bottom-thickness text again.

Older free copies circulating online, such as the 2003 text, limited the internal interval to 10 years when corrosion rates were unknown and capped it at 20 years in any case. Later editions added an initial internal inspection interval table that starts from a base interval and adds credits for safeguards such as a release prevention barrier, a bottom lining, cathodic protection and bottom design details. Industry summaries of the current edition describe the initial interval as capped at 20 years without a release prevention barrier and 30 years with one. Treat those numbers as secondary until you have checked them in your licensed copy and addenda. The 2003 text also allowed an owner/operator to use an RBI assessment to raise or lower the corrosion-rate interval, including the 20-year figure, provided an authorized inspector and an engineer experienced in tank design and corrosion approved it and re-reviewed it at least every 10 years. Check how your current edition frames this, because summaries differ.

Two points are often missed. First, API 653 allows the bottom to be assessed with the tank in service when that is the sole purpose of the internal inspection, using robotic ultrasonic thickness measurement and other on-stream methods, with electromagnetic methods as a supplement. The data must be good enough to establish thickness, corrosion rate and integrity, and the responsible authorized inspector must assure its quality. Second, regulation can remove options the standard allows. PHMSA's breakout-tank rule for hazardous liquid pipelines (49 CFR 195.432) requires API 653 for atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks but does not allow the standard's alternative (RBI) internal interval clause to be used.

The calculation families API 653 inspectors work through

Most API 653 decisions come down to a handful of calculations: corrosion rate and remaining life, minimum shell thickness and maximum fill height, evaluation of corroded areas and pits, minimum bottom and annular plate thickness, settlement limits, and hydrotest thickness for reconstructed tanks.

API's published body of knowledge for the API 653 exam lists the calculation families an inspector is expected to perform, which is a useful public map of what the standard actually asks for:

  • Corrosion rate and remaining life. Corrosion rate is the previous thickness minus the current thickness, divided by the years between them. Remaining life is the current thickness minus the minimum allowable thickness, divided by the corrosion rate. These two numbers drive the external, ultrasonic and internal intervals described above.
  • Minimum shell thickness and maximum fill height. The shell minimum thickness formula uses tank diameter, liquid height, specific gravity of the product, allowable stress and joint efficiency. Rearranged, the same formula gives the maximum allowable liquid height for a shell with a known minimum thickness. This is how a thin course leads to a lower operating level rather than an immediate repair.
  • Corroded areas and pitting on the shell. The standard defines how to average thickness over a critical length for a corroded area, how to compare the least thickness exclusive of pits, and how to evaluate widely scattered pits by depth and by total length within a vertical band.
  • Bottom and annular plate minimum thickness. Bottom plates are judged against the minimum thickness table at the next inspection, accounting for both product-side and soil-side corrosion; annular plate rings have their own requirements.
  • Settlement. Annex B of API 653 (see tank settlement measurement and acceptance) covers settlement evaluation: uniform and planar tilt, out-of-plane (differential) settlement of the shell, edge settlement, bottom settlement near the shell, and localized bottom settlement remote from the shell. The number of survey points around the shell is also defined.

Qualitative worked example: a 1970s crude tank shows lower course thickness readings below the previous survey on the external UT programme. The authorized inspector computes the corrosion rate from the two surveys, finds that the course still exceeds its minimum thickness at the current fill height, and calculates that remaining life supports the next survey at the RCA/2N interval rather than five years. At the same time, an area of local pitting near the bottom-to-shell weld is evaluated with the corroded-area and pitting rules. If it passes, it is recorded and monitored; if not, the owner can lower the maximum fill height, schedule a repair, or ask an engineer for a fitness-for-service assessment. The inspection data do not change. What changes is the decision the owner and inspector make from them. Ask us to scope the shell and floor NDE your inspector needs for these calculations.

Repairs, alterations, reconstruction and the hydrotest question

API 653 distinguishes repairs (work to restore a tank to a safe operating condition) from alterations (changes to physical dimensions or configuration) and reconstruction (reassembling a dismantled tank), and it sets material, welding, NDE and testing requirements for each.

Repair and alteration work under API 653 refers back to API 650 at almost every step. New repair materials must meet the current edition of API 650, weld procedures and welders are qualified to ASME Section IX with API 650/653 supplements, and NDE is performed in accordance with API 650 with any supplemental requirements in API 653. Every newly deposited weld, and every cavity from gouging or grinding, is visually examined over its full length, with additional examination depending on the repair type.

Common repair categories in the standard include shell plate replacement and inserts, lap-welded patch plates where permitted, shell penetrations and nozzles, tank bottom replacement or partial replacement (including new bottoms over old ones), annular plate repairs, roof repairs, floating roof seal replacement, and hot taps. Each has its own detail rules for weld spacing, plate thickness and examination.

The hydrostatic test question is one of the most common reasons people search API 653. In short, major repairs and alterations normally require a full hydrostatic test, but the standard allows certain repairs to be exempted when specific conditions are met, and that exemption must be reviewed and approved by an engineer experienced in tank design under the standard's rules. Reconstructed tanks are hydrotested. Because the exemption criteria are detailed and edition-specific, they must be read in the current text, not recalled from memory.

Records close the loop. The standard expects nameplate updates for reconstructed or re-rated tanks and a permanent record of inspections, repairs and alterations, including the calculations behind the next inspection date.

The API 653 document family: 650, 575, 651, 652, 571 and STI SP001

API 650 builds the tank; API 653 keeps it in service; API RP 575 explains inspection practice; API RP 651 and RP 652 cover cathodic protection and bottom linings; STI SP001 is the common alternative for shop-built and smaller tanks.

API's published body of knowledge for the API 653 inspector exam lists much the same set: selected RP 571 mechanisms, RP 575, RP 576, RP 577, API 653 with related parts of API 650, RP 651, RP 652, and ASME Sections V and IX.

Regulations that point to API 653: SPCC, PSM, PHMSA and Canada

API 653 is an industry standard, but regulations frequently make it the yardstick: EPA SPCC integrity testing, OSHA PSM mechanical integrity, and PHMSA rules for pipeline breakout tanks all lean on it. Confirm what applies to your facility with the relevant agency.

  • EPA SPCC (40 CFR 112). For onshore facilities subject to the Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure rule, each aboveground container must be tested or inspected for integrity on a regular schedule and whenever material repairs are made, with frequency, type of testing and qualifications of personnel set according to industry standards. API 653 is the industry standard most field-erected tanks are inspected against; STI SP001 is common for shop-built tanks.
  • OSHA PSM (29 CFR 1910.119). Where a tank is part of a covered process, it falls under the mechanical integrity element, which requires inspection and testing that follows recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices (RAGAGEP), at frequencies consistent with good engineering practice, with each inspection documented. API 653 is the RAGAGEP most plants cite for atmospheric tanks.
  • PHMSA breakout tanks (49 CFR 195.432). Hazardous liquid pipeline operators inspect each in-service breakout tank at intervals not exceeding 15 months, at least once each calendar year, and use API 653 (without its RBI interval option) for physical integrity.
  • State and local rules. Some states and fire marshals have their own storage tank rules or adopt API 653 by reference. Check with the state environmental agency and fire authority.
  • Canada. Provincial environmental, fire-code and petroleum storage regulations govern tanks, and many owners adopt API 653 as their in-service standard. Requirements vary by province; confirm with the provincial authority having jurisdiction.

Common API 653 mistakes we see in tank programmes

The usual failures are administrative rather than technical: no defensible corrosion rate, intervals copied from another tank, MFL data with no UT prove-up, settlement never surveyed, and nobody clearly named as the authorized inspector.

  • Using a default interval instead of a calculated one. A five-year external inspection is a maximum, not a target. When RCA/4N is shorter, the shorter interval applies.
  • Treating MFL as a thickness measurement. MFL screens; UT sizes (see MFL vs UT floor scanning). Reports that list MFL "percent loss" with no UT confirmation are hard to defend.
  • Ignoring the critical zone and annular ring. The area near the shell is where bottoms fail and where floor scanners struggle. Plan supplementary UT or scanning there.
  • No baseline. Without an earlier thickness survey the corrosion rate is unknown, which pushes the interval to the conservative unknown-rate limits.
  • Repair without an engineering check. Hydrotest exemptions, lap patches and hot taps each have conditions. Get the engineer's approval documented before the welding starts.

How Atlantis supports API 653 programmes

Atlantis performs the NDE that an API 653 programme needs: external UT thickness surveys, shell and annular-plate corrosion mapping, MFL tank-floor scanning with UT prove-up, vacuum-box testing, and MT, PT and RT on repair welds, by ASNT-certified technicians under ASNT Level III oversight. Results go to the owner's API 653 authorized inspector, who stays inspector of record and sets intervals and repair decisions. More API 653 questions

What does "tank inspection, repair, alteration, and reconstruction" mean?

It is the full title of API Standard 653. Inspection covers routine, external, ultrasonic and internal inspections; repair restores a tank to a safe condition; alteration changes its dimensions or configuration; reconstruction covers dismantling and re-erecting a tank, including relocation.

Is API 653 required by law?

Not universally. API 653 is an industry standard, but EPA SPCC, OSHA PSM and PHMSA breakout-tank rules rely on industry standards for tank integrity, and PHMSA's rule names API 653 directly. State rules may also reference it. Confirm with your regulator.

Does API 653 cover shop-built tanks?

Owners may apply API 653 to any steel tank built to a tank specification, but many shop-fabricated and smaller tanks are inspected under STI SP001, particularly for SPCC. The owner chooses the standard and must be able to justify it. Tell us about your tanks and we will propose the NDE scope your authorized inspector needs.
